SK2222 The type declares checked for some of its operators and not the rest

A type declares a user-defined checked operator for one of its arithmetic operators and not for another that has a checked form, so inside one checked block overflow throws on one operator of that type and silently wraps on the next.

CategoryCorrectness
Default severitywarning
ScopeSemantic
Needs a compilationyes
Runs under --load=looseno
Cached per fileyes
Fixno
Language version floorC# 11.0
Since2.0

Why

⚠ "This type has no checked operator" is an observation; "this type has checked on some operators and not others" is a defect, and the difference is the entire specification. A type that declares no checked operator has simply not opted into C# 11's user-defined checked arithmetic, and checked around it means what it always meant — there is nothing to report and no way to know whether overflow matters here. A type that declares operator checked + and not operator checked - has stated, in its own source, that overflow on this type is meant to trap; and then checked(a - b) wraps silently on the line below the checked(a + b) that throws. The evidence for the author's intent comes from the type itself, so the rule never has to guess.

Example

Instead of:

public static Money operator +(Money a, Money b) => …;
public static Money operator checked +(Money a, Money b) => …;
public static Money operator -(Money a, Money b) => …;   // no checked form

Write:

public static Money operator -(Money a, Money b) => …;
public static Money operator checked -(Money a, Money b) => …;

When it does not fire

⚠ A type declaring no checked operator at all is never reported, and that is the guard the rule is built around. Nearly every type with a user-defined + is in that position, and reporting them would be an opinion about whether overflow matters on somebody else's type — which nothing in the source answers. The rule fires only where the type has already answered it.

⚠ The eight operators that have a checked form are listed, and the list was measured against the compiler rather than remembered. Binary +, -, *, /; unary -; ++; --; and the explicit conversion. Every other operator is rejected outright by the language: CS9023 for unary +, %, &, << and ==, and CS9024 for an implicit conversion. Naming any of those would be asking for a declaration that does not compile.

⚠ The opposite direction is already a compiler error and is not restated. operator checked + with no matching unchecked + is CS9025. Only the direction the compiler is silent about is this rule's subject.

Parameter and return types are compared, not just the operator name. A type may overload + several times — Money + Money and Money + long — and a checked form of one says nothing about the other; matching on name alone would call a genuinely missing counterpart present. Two explicit conversions from the same type are distinguished by their return type for the same reason. The rule is silent below C# 11, where no checked operator can be declared at all.

⚠ `resharperId` is deliberately null even though `OperatorWithoutMatchedCheckedOperator` exists. That inspection reports every unmatched operator; this rule reports the inconsistent subset, which is a fraction of it. Claiming the inspection in the parity map would credit Skala with coverage it does not have and would move the inspection out of the measured residue, so the inspection stays counted as uncovered and this rule claims nothing.

⚠ No fix. The repair is a second operator body, and whether the checked form should throw, saturate or clamp is the design question the finding is asking about — not something an edit to one file's text can decide.
